oh boy.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this book.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The story of the series so far.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie found a magic tree house full of books. If they point to a picture in a book, they can go to that time and place. No time passes at home while they are away.

background.note: Frog Creek is a made-up town. Pennsylvania is a real U.S. state in the northeast, where the author grew up for some years.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie eventually found out that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay,
paragraphs.simple: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from Camelot. Jack and Annie have done many missions for Morgan and Merlin. Teddy and Kathleen, two young enchanters, sometimes help them.

background.note: Camelot is King Arthur's castle and kingdom in old British stories.
Merlin is the most famous magician in the King Arthur stories. Books 29 and later in this series are called "Merlin Missions".

paragraphs.context: Annie slipped into the house to tell their parents.
paragraphs.simple: Annie goes in to tell their parents. Jack puts down his book. He is tired from swimming, but happy. A bike ride in the warm evening seems perfect.

background.note: Jack loves reading about animals. In the series he always carries a notebook and likes facts.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran down the porch steps and climbed on their bikes.
paragraphs.simple: They put on their helmets and ride up the street. They wave to a woman cutting her grass and to two people walking their dogs.

paragraphs.context: “Well, both. I want a little dog and a big dog,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants a small dog, a big dog, and maybe a middle-sized dog too. Jack would like just one.
paragraphs.tone: A light, funny talk. It hints that this book will be about dogs.

paragraphs.context: “Not kidding! I had a feeling, even before we left the house!” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie saw a flash of light over the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is not joking. She rides her bike off the sidewalk and into the woods.

paragraphs.context: Jack followed, his bike bouncing over roots and twigs in the shadows beneath the trees.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's bike jumps over roots and small sticks. It is getting dark, and crickets are singing.

paragraphs.context: The magic tree house was perched high in the oak.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy is waiting in the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house sits high in the tree. Teddy smiles from the window. He says he was going to send a crow or a rabbit to get them.

background.note: In the Merlin Missions, Teddy is a young enchanter from Camelot. (In books 17–20 he was under a spell as a little dog.)

paragraphs.context: “Where? A seaside town in a vast territory below the Arctic,” said Teddy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Where and when they are going.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy says they will go to a town by the sea in a huge land just south of the Arctic, in February 1925. Merlin and Morgan think they can save lives there.

background.note: In February, Nome gets only a few hours of daylight, and it is often −30 °C or colder.
Nome is about 2° south of the Arctic Circle, the line around the far north of the Earth.

paragraphs.context: “Alaska? Oh, boy, I’ve always wanted to visit Alaska,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: The travel guide is about Alaska. It was printed in 1925, so it shows Alaska as it was then.

background.note: Alaska is the biggest U.S. state, in the far northwest of North America. It is very cold in winter. The U.S. bought it from Russia in 1867. It became a state in 1959.

paragraphs.context: “No! Don’t open it now,” said Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: The gold box holds a tiny bit of magic gold dust from Morgan. They can use it only once.

paragraphs.context: “In your time of need, you can use it to acquire a great skill that you both will share,” said Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: When they really need it, the gold dust will give both of them a great skill.

paragraphs.context: “Cool!” said Annie. “Like the time we used the magic mist of Avalon
paragraphs.simple: Annie and Jack remember other times when magic gave them a skill: rock climbing, magic tricks, training horses and playing soccer.

background.note: Avalon is a magic island in the King Arthur stories. In earlier Merlin Missions, Morgan gave Jack and Annie a "mist of Avalon" for special skills.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, a bit like all those times,” said Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: Before, the magic lasted one hour. This time it will last twelve hours.

paragraphs.context: “But there is another difference,” said Teddy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The skill is only to help others.
paragraphs.simple: On earlier missions the skill helped Jack and Annie themselves. This time they can use it only to save other people's lives.

paragraphs.context: “One more thing,” said Teddy. “Merlin wants those you help on this mission to be celebrated as heroes.
paragraphs.simple: Merlin wants the people they help to be called heroes. He does not want anyone to know that magic helped.

paragraphs.context: Teddy reached into his cloak and brought out a second tiny box.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy gives Annie a tiny box of shiny dark blue stone. It holds very rare and valuable stardust.

paragraphs.context: “If you toss the stardust into the air and make a wish to be forgotten,” said Teddy,
paragraphs.simple: If they throw the stardust into the air and wish to be forgotten, everyone will forget their visit, and nothing will show they were there.

paragraphs.context: “Be safe. Be well,” said Teddy. “And do not freeze to death.”
paragraphs.simple: Teddy says goodbye and tells them not to die from the cold. Jack jokes: "Thanks, good advice."
paragraphs.tone: Funny. Jack's "Gee, thanks" means the advice is a little scary.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house spins and then stops. Nothing moves.
paragraphs.tone: Every trip in the series starts with these same short lines.

paragraphs.context: “Cold…face,” Annie said, her teeth chattering.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is very cold in Alaska.
paragraphs.simple: Annie's face is so cold that she can hardly talk. Her teeth knock together.

background.note: Your body shakes when it is cold (shivering). This makes heat, and it can make your teeth knock together.

paragraphs.context: Jack laughed. He and Annie were covered with fur from head to toe.
paragraphs.simple: Magic has dressed them in fur pants, gloves, high boots and long coats with hoods.

background.note: Native Alaskan people made warm clothes from the fur and skins of animals like seals, caribou and reindeer.

paragraphs.context: The tree house had landed in one of a few trees at the edge of a snowy field.
paragraphs.simple: Near the tree house is a snowy field. Past the field is a town by the sea. The sun is going down over a sea covered with ice.

paragraphs.context: About 12,000 years ago, people and their dogs crossed a land bridge over the Bering Sea from Russia into Alaska.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the guide: the first people in Alaska.
paragraphs.simple: About 12,000 years ago, people and their dogs walked from Asia (Russia) to Alaska over land that is now under the sea. They were the first people and dogs in North America.

background.note: The Bering Sea lies between Russia and Alaska. At its narrowest (the Bering Strait), Asia and America are only about 80 km apart.

paragraphs.context: Until Russian explorers came to Alaska a few hundred years ago, only native Alaskan people lived there.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the guide: Native Alaskans.
paragraphs.simple: Before Russian explorers came, only native Alaskan people lived there. They lived for thousands of years using the few things the cold, rocky land gave them.

background.note: Native Alaskan peoples include the Inupiat, Yupik, Aleut, Athabascan, Tlingit and others. Near Nome, many people were Inupiat.
Vitus Bering, a Danish explorer working for Russia, reached Alaska in 1741. Russians then came to hunt sea otters for their fur.

paragraphs.context: In the late 1800s, the United States purchased Alaska from Russia, and it became a territory of the U.S.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the guide: the U.S. buys Alaska.
paragraphs.simple: In 1867 the U.S. bought Alaska from Russia. It became a U.S. territory, not yet a state.

background.note: The U.S. paid $7.2 million for Alaska, about 2 cents an acre. Many people thought it was a silly buy at first.
A territory belonged to the U.S. but did not have the full rights of a state. Alaska became the 49th state in 1959.

paragraphs.context: “Gold dust, stardust,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sums up: gold dust to save lives, stardust to make everyone forget they saved lives.

paragraphs.context: As Annie started down the tree house ladder, Jack crammed the Alaska guide into another one of his pockets.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushes the guide into a pocket and climbs down slowly. His thick clothes make him clumsy.

paragraphs.context: As they started across the snow-covered field, their boots squeaked in the snow.
paragraphs.simple: Their boots make little sounds in the snow. The dry, cold air hurts Jack's throat.

background.note: Very cold, dry snow squeaks when you walk on it. It happens when it is colder than about −10 °C.

paragraphs.context: In the fading winter light, they crossed a bridge and walked along a frozen creek
paragraphs.simple: In the last light of day, they walk to a wooden path by the frozen sea. The street is empty. There are only piles of ice and snow.

background.note: Nome had wooden sidewalks (boardwalks) because the streets were mud in summer and snow in winter.

paragraphs.context: As Jack and Annie tramped through the snow, they passed stores and saloons and restaurants
paragraphs.simple: Many shops have broken windows and look left empty. Only a few shops may still be open: a drugstore, a laundry and a bakery.

background.note: A saloon was a bar where people drank alcohol. Gold rush towns had many of them.

paragraphs.context: Around 1900, gold was discovered in Nome, a remote Alaskan town on the Bering Sea.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the guide: Nome's gold rush.
paragraphs.simple: About 1900 people found gold in Nome. Over 30,000 people hurried there. Ten years later the gold was gone, and the town became poor.

background.note: Nome is a small town on the west coast of Alaska, on the Bering Sea. In winter the sea freezes, so in 1925 no ships could reach it.
In 1898 three men (the "Three Lucky Swedes") found gold near Nome. Gold was even found in the beach sand.

paragraphs.context: “Hard times? No kidding,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nome looks like a ghost town.
paragraphs.simple: Annie agrees the town looks very poor. It looks more like an empty town than a busy, growing town.

paragraphs.context: Finally, they came to a white two-story wooden building
paragraphs.simple: A two-story wooden house is the town hospital (MAYNARD-COLUMBUS HOSPITAL). It has lights and people inside. The cinema and the hotel had signs saying "TEMPORARILY CLOSED".

background.note: The Maynard-Columbus Hospital was Nome's real hospital in 1925. It had only a few beds. Dr. Curtis Welch was the only doctor in the area.

paragraphs.context: They walked down the boardwalk until they came to a schoolhouse
paragraphs.mainIdea: The school is closed because of a quarantine.
paragraphs.simple: The sign says NO SCHOOL. QUARANTINE. The school is closed. People must stay home so a disease does not spread.

background.note: In January 1925 Dr. Welch closed the schools, churches and cinema in Nome to stop the disease from spreading.

paragraphs.context: In the twilight, Jack and Annie hurried up the boardwalk to the entrance of the small hospital.
paragraphs.simple: The waiting room is cold and full of people in fur coats. Some are very sick. Others look sad, as if they were waiting for someone else.

paragraphs.context: “Are you sick with diphtheria?” the boy said.
paragraphs.simple: The boy asks if they are sick with diphtheria.

background.note: Diphtheria makes a thick gray layer grow in the throat, so people cannot breathe. In 1925 it killed many children. A medicine called antitoxin (serum) could save them.

paragraphs.context: “It’s a dangerous disease from the past. That must be what the quarantine is for,” Jack whispered.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie cannot catch it.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says diphtheria is a disease from long ago. They cannot get it, because they had vaccine shots.

background.note: Today most children get a vaccine (often called DTP or DTaP) that protects them from diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough.

paragraphs.context: “No. My sister and my mother do,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boy's sister and mother are sick.
paragraphs.simple: The boy's sister and mother are very sick. He is waiting for a special medicine. The doctor says it will save them.

background.note: There was antitoxin in Nome, but it was old (from 1918) and there was too little. New serum had to come from Anchorage, over 1,000 miles away.

paragraphs.context: Two people were anxiously watching a man talk on an old-fashioned black telephone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mayor talks on the telephone.
paragraphs.simple: Mayor Maynard asks on the phone if the dog-sled driver has arrived with the medicine.

background.note: Mushers drove dog sleds. In 1925 Alaska had few roads, and in winter dog sleds carried mail and goods. The word may come from the French "marche!" (go!).

paragraphs.context: “No, listen to me!” Mayor Maynard yelled into the phone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mayor wants the medicine to wait.
paragraphs.simple: The mayor says: if Gunnar Kaasen gets to the roadhouse in Solomon, keep him there. A big snowstorm is coming. They cannot risk losing the medicine.

background.note: Gunnar Kaasen was a real Norwegian musher. He drove the last long part of the 1925 medicine run, with Balto leading his dog team.

paragraphs.context: “We cannot lose that medicine!” said the mayor.
paragraphs.simple: Five people have died. Twenty or more are sick, maybe fifty. The health officials think waiting is better than losing the medicine.

background.note: A Board of Health is a group of officials who make rules to protect people's health in a town.

paragraphs.context: “No! You can’t delay it!” the boy said, barging into the office.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oki does not want to wait.
paragraphs.simple: The boy runs into the office. He says the musher must not stop. The medicine must come soon.

paragraphs.context: The boy turned to a large rosy-cheeked woman.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oki asks the nurse for help.
paragraphs.simple: Oki asks Nurse Morgan not to let them wait. He is almost crying.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry,” said a gray-haired man in a white coat.
paragraphs.simple: Dr. Welch says everyone is working all the time to fight the disease.

background.note: An epidemic is when a disease spreads to many people in one area at the same time.

paragraphs.context: “You must leave us to do our work,” said Dr. Welch.
paragraphs.simple: Dr. Welch kindly takes Oki back to the hall and tells him to rest. Then he closes the door.

paragraphs.context: “It sounds like medicine is on the way,” Jack said, trying to calm him.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the medicine is coming and will arrive after the storm. Oki says it must come as soon as possible.

paragraphs.context: “The doctor can do nothing until the medicine arrives,” Oki said.
paragraphs.simple: Oki says he can do something himself. He walks quickly out of the hospital into the dark, and very cold air blows in.

paragraphs.context: “Our mission! Help save the lives of these sick people!” Annie said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks their mission is to help save the sick people. That is why Merlin sent them.

paragraphs.context: “He will be! He’s going to do something crazy. I can feel it!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie feels that Oki will do something dangerous. She runs out of the hospital, and Jack follows. The moon is full and bright.
paragraphs.tone: Annie often trusts her feelings, and she is often right.

paragraphs.context: Annie and Jack fell into step beside him.
paragraphs.simple: Annie and Jack walk next to Oki. Annie says they came to help fight the disease.

paragraphs.context: “No plane can fly at forty or fifty degrees below zero!” said Oki.
paragraphs.simple: Oki says planes cannot fly in such cold; the pilot would freeze. Jack thinks planes then had open cockpits.

background.term: forty or fifty degrees below zero
background.note: These are Fahrenheit degrees. −40 °F is the same as −40 °C; −50 °F is about −46 °C.
Early planes had open cockpits with no roof, so the pilot sat in the wind. In 1925 there was almost no flying in Alaska in winter.

paragraphs.context: “No roads in winter,” said Oki. “The only way to Nome is by dogsled, over the mail trail.”
paragraphs.simple: In winter there are no roads, and the sea is frozen. The only way to reach Nome is by dogsled on the mail trail.

background.note: The Iditarod Trail was the winter mail route to Nome. Dog teams carried mail and goods on it. Today the famous Iditarod sled dog race follows part of this trail.

paragraphs.context: “I will take a team of dogs and find Gunnar Kaasen,” said Oki.
paragraphs.simple: Oki plans to take a dog team through the storm, find Kaasen and bring the medicine himself.

paragraphs.context: “My uncle Joe is a mail carrier,” said Oki.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oki's uncle has a dog team.
paragraphs.simple: Oki's uncle Joe carries mail with his dog team. He has a broken leg, so he cannot go. Oki says he is not afraid to go alone.

paragraphs.context: In the bright moonlight, Jack could see that the shack was made of old driftwood and flattened tin cans.
paragraphs.simple: The small house is made of old wood from the sea and flat metal cans. Smoke comes out of a pipe on the roof.

paragraphs.context: Next to the small house was a dog pen surrounded by a wire fence.
paragraphs.simple: There is a fenced place for the dogs. Eight huskies sleep close together in the snow to stay warm.

background.note: Alaskan huskies are strong, fast sled dogs. Their thick fur and the way they curl up (with the tail over the nose) keep them warm at very low temperatures.

paragraphs.context: But Annie had an instant connection with the dogs.
paragraphs.simple: The dogs like Annie at once. She pets their furry heads and asks their names.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, Annie has a special way with animals,” said Jack. “Especially dogs.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says Annie is very good with animals. Oki smiles for the first time and asks them in.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie followed the Alaskan boy into the shack.
paragraphs.simple: The room is cold and smells of fish and lamp oil. Music plays on an old wooden radio.

background.note: In 1925 radio was new and exciting. Families sat around big wooden radio sets to hear music and news.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie looked around. Strips of dried dark pink fish hung from a rack near the stove,
paragraphs.simple: Dried fish hangs near a stove made from an old metal barrel. Wooden barrels are used as chairs.

background.note: Dried salmon was an important food in Alaska for people and for sled dogs.

paragraphs.context: Jack wondered if he and Annie should leave. It seemed wrong to overhear a family argument.
paragraphs.simple: Oki and his uncle are arguing in the next room. Jack thinks they should go outside, but Annie wants to help.

paragraphs.context: The music had stopped. A news bulletin had come on:
paragraphs.simple: The radio says a very serious event is happening in Nome.

background.note: Radio news made the serum run famous. People across America listened every day to hear if the medicine had arrived.

paragraphs.context: “All eyes are on this small icebound town in the northern territory,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The radio tells about the medicine relay.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone is watching Nome. Diphtheria has killed five people. Twenty mushers and more than 160 dogs are passing the medicine from team to team over 600 miles, from Nenana to Nome.

background.note: Nenana is a town in central Alaska. The medicine came there by train from Anchorage, and the dog teams carried it from Nenana to Nome.
About 1,085 km (674 miles). The teams did it in about five and a half days. Usually the mail took about 25 days.

paragraphs.context: “But now a blizzard threatens to curtail the efforts to save the residents of Nome,” the announcer said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The storm may stop the relay.
paragraphs.simple: A big storm is coming with strong winds and very low temperatures. It may stop the people trying to save Nome.

background.note: −30 °F is about −34 °C. In the real storm, it was colder: sometimes about −40 °F/°C or colder with the wind.
About 65 km/h. Strong wind makes cold air feel much colder ("wind chill").

paragraphs.context: “It is unclear whether the mushers and their teams of heroic dogs will be able to continue,” the announcer said.
paragraphs.simple: Nobody knows if the teams can go on. Now Gunnar Kaasen has the medicine. His lead dog is Balto.

background.note: Balto (1919–1933) was a black Siberian husky. He led Gunnar Kaasen's team on the last part of the run into Nome and became very famous.

paragraphs.context: “Balto!” said Annie. “Didn’t we see a statue of him in Central Park in New York?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers a statue of Balto in New York, but they do not remember why he is famous.

background.term: statue of him in Central Park
background.note: A bronze statue of Balto has stood in Central Park, New York, since December 1925. Balto himself came to see it being opened.

paragraphs.context: “Will the blizzard keep the medicine from getting to the sick and dying in Nome?” the announcer said.
paragraphs.simple: The man on the radio asks if the storm will stop the medicine. Then he happily starts the music again.

background.note: Joe "King" Oliver led a famous early jazz band. Young Louis Armstrong played trumpet in it.

paragraphs.context: The lively music came back on, and Oki turned the radio off.
paragraphs.simple: Oki turns off the radio and fills a bag with dried fish for the dogs.

background.note: Burlap is a rough cloth made from plant fibers (jute). It was used for bags of rice, coffee and potatoes.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie turned to see a native Alaskan man hobbling into the room on a crutch.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe walks in on a crutch. He has long black hair and a face marked by the weather. He looks only at Oki and says Oki cannot go if Kaasen and Balto cannot.

background.note: Jet is a hard, shiny black stone used in jewelry, so "jet-black" means very black.

paragraphs.context: “Do not go out there alone, Oki,” rasped his uncle.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe says Oki is not a great musher like Seppala or Kaasen, and his dogs are not as strong as Togo or Balto.

background.note: Leonhard Seppala was a famous Norwegian-born musher. He and his lead dog Togo ran the longest and most dangerous part of the relay, about 260 miles there and back.
Togo was Seppala's lead dog. Many people think Togo was the real hero of the run, but Balto got the fame.

paragraphs.context: Jack held his breath as he looked back and forth from Oki to his uncle.
paragraphs.simple: Jack watches Oki and his uncle. He stops Annie from speaking. He thinks it is not their business.

paragraphs.context: “Who will help you in a whiteout?” his uncle asked.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe asks who will help Oki in a whiteout or if the ice breaks and floats out to sea.

background.note: The trail went across the frozen sea (Norton Sound) to save time. Sometimes the ice broke and floated away, which was very dangerous.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe. But what about my mother?” Oki cried.
paragraphs.simple: Oki says his mother and sister cannot breathe or swallow and have a high fever. He promised them the medicine.
paragraphs.tone: Very emotional. Oki is scared for his family.

paragraphs.context: “Stay with me, boy!” Uncle Joe called after Oki.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe calls Oki back, but the dogs bark so loudly that nobody hears him.

paragraphs.context: “Jack and Annie,” said Annie. “We’re friends of Oki’s, and—and—we’re champion mushers.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they are very good mushers. Jack is surprised, but then he remembers the gold dust.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. He was a little nervous about losing their way and freezing to death,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack agrees, though he is nervous.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is worried about getting lost and freezing, but he nods.

paragraphs.context: The man stared at them for a moment, his face lined with grief.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe lost his wife and two children in the flu epidemic seven years before. More than a thousand people in Nome died then.

background.note: The 1918 flu ("Spanish flu") killed about 50 million people around the world. It hit native Alaskan villages very badly; some villages lost most of their people.

paragraphs.context: “Thank you. But please leave my nephew here,” said the man.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Joe asks them to keep Oki home.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe asks them not to let Oki go. Oki and his mother and sister are his only family.

paragraphs.context: “Take my team. They are good dogs,” said Oki’s uncle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Joe lends them his dogs.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe says the dogs know the trail well because they have carried mail on it hundreds of times.

paragraphs.context: Jack poured a bit of the gold dust into the palm of his bare hand.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wishes for them to become champion dog mushers to save lives. He throws the dust in the air. Gold light shines around them and then goes away.

background.note: Magic objects from Morgan and Merlin appear in many Merlin Missions. They often give a skill for a short time.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Jack. “The magic works for twelve hours.”
paragraphs.simple: The magic lasts twelve hours. It is 8:30 p.m., so they must be back by 8:30 the next morning.

background.note: 8:30 p.m. plus 12 hours = 8:30 a.m. the next morning.

paragraphs.context: “Yes!” said Annie. “You have to stay here. He can’t risk losing you.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie say Uncle Joe wants them to take the team and Oki to stay. Oki says they do not know the dogs or the trail.

paragraphs.context: “Good! Then our job is just to help them do their job,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the dogs know the job; they only need to help them. Jack says Oki's job is to stay near his family.

paragraphs.context: Oki stared out toward the frozen sea for a moment. He looked very troubled.
paragraphs.simple: Oki wants to go, but he stays for his uncle. He opens the gate for Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: “Come on, guys,” Jack said to the huskies. “Let’s buckle up!”
paragraphs.simple: Even in the dark, they put the harnesses on the dogs easily. The magic skill is working.

background.note: A sled dog harness goes around the dog's chest and back, so it can pull with its whole body without hurting its neck.

paragraphs.context: When Jack and Annie finished putting harnesses on all the dogs, they hooked the team to the rigging.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joining the dogs to the sled.
paragraphs.simple: They join the dogs to the ropes. Tug lines go to the harnesses, and neck lines go to the collars.

background.note: On a dog team, each dog's tug line joins its harness to the main rope (the gangline or towline), so the dog can pull. The neck line joins its collar to the main rope to keep it in place.

paragraphs.context: Jack laughed. He knew not to scold the dogs and risk dampening their enthusiasm.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not shout at the dogs. They need to stay happy and excited for the hard run.

paragraphs.context: Soon all the huskies were strung to the towline, lined up in pairs.
paragraphs.simple: The eight dogs stand in pairs. The two lead dogs are in front, with their tails up. Bells ring on their collars.

background.note: Most dog teams run in pairs side by side on a long gangline (towline). Sometimes one lead dog runs alone, like Balto.

paragraphs.context: Two swing dogs stood behind the leads.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The places in a dog team.
paragraphs.simple: From front to back: two lead dogs, two swing dogs, two team dogs, and two wheel dogs next to the sled.

background.note: Wheel dogs are usually big and strong, because they pull the sled around corners and out of deep snow.

paragraphs.context: “Be firm. Be fair. Give kindness and respect,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they are firm, fair, kind and respectful with dogs.

paragraphs.context: “About thirty-five miles,” said Oki.
paragraphs.simple: Solomon is about 35 miles (56 km) away. Port Safety is on the way, at about 20 miles. The trip there takes about five hours.

background.note: Port Safety was a roadhouse (a small inn for travelers) on the trail about 21 miles from Nome. It was the last stop before Nome in the relay.

paragraphs.context: “Okey dokey,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sits in the basket of the sled and holds the sides. Jack will drive first.

paragraphs.context: Jack stepped onto the long runners that extended behind the basket.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stands on the two long pieces at the back of the sled and holds the handles. He feels as if he has driven a dogsled all his life.

background.note: A musher stands on the back ends of the runners and pushes or runs to help the dogs on hills.

paragraphs.context: “I’ll get the snow hook,” said Oki.
paragraphs.simple: Oki gives them the metal hook that holds the sled in place, and the bag of dried fish for the dogs.

paragraphs.context: “Line out!” Jack called to the dogs, knowing all the right commands to use.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows all the commands. The lead dogs pull the line straight. Then the whole team runs into the night.

background.note: Mushers use special words. "Line out" tells the lead dog to stand and keep the line tight. "Hike!" means go; "Gee!" means turn right; "Haw!" means turn left; "Whoa!" means stop.

paragraphs.context: Moonlight cast a silvery glow over the icebound sea.
paragraphs.simple: The moon shines on the frozen sea. The only sounds are the dogs' breathing, the bells, the sled creaking and the runners on the snow.

paragraphs.context: As the dogs did their job, Jack magically knew how to do his:
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows exactly how to drive: how to push with one foot, keep the right speed so the dogs do not hurt their lungs, balance on bumps, and keep the lines tight.

paragraphs.context: Jack knew all the musher commands, too.
paragraphs.simple: "Gee!" turns the team right, "Haw!" turns it left, and "Straight ahead!" makes the line straight again.

background.note: Nobody knows exactly where "gee" and "haw" come from. Farmers used the same words to turn horses and oxen.

paragraphs.context: Every time the dogs did what Jack commanded, he said, “Good dogs!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack praises the dogs but says little. Dogs need short, clear commands.

paragraphs.context: “Wow!” is right, Jack thought. The windless Alaskan night was beautiful.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maybe the storm will not come.
paragraphs.simple: The night is calm and beautiful. Jack hopes the weather report was wrong.

paragraphs.context: Mile after mile, the huskies ran along the well-worn trail.
paragraphs.simple: Going down a hill, Jack drags his heel to slow the dogs. Going up, he jumps off and runs to make the sled lighter.

background.note: Dragging your foot or heel slows a sled. Mushers also use a brake (a metal claw) and a drag mat.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled. He loved being a champion musher.
paragraphs.simple: Jack loves knowing what to do, and he loves his close feeling with the dogs. He almost feels like a running dog himself.

paragraphs.context: Jack realized it had gotten colder and darker.
paragraphs.simple: Clouds hide the moon. Wind blows and snow falls. Snow freezes on Jack's glasses, and he cannot see.

background.term: Snowflakes began to freeze on the lenses
background.note: Glasses are a problem in great cold: breath freezes on them, and metal frames can stick to skin.

paragraphs.context: As the huskies headed into a sharp curve, Jack lost his balance.
paragraphs.simple: At a sharp turn Jack falls off the sled into the snow. The dogs stop and bark.

paragraphs.context: “I guess I was too sure of myself,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks he was too confident. Annie says everyone has problems if they cannot see. She drives now.

paragraphs.context: The huskies started running again.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cleans his glasses with his bare fingers, but the cold hurts his skin, so he puts his mitten back on.

paragraphs.context: Annie kept a steady hand and a steady pace as she drove the eight huskies through the snowstorm.
paragraphs.simple: Annie drives calmly at an even speed. She moves her weight so the sled does not fall over. Jack leans to help on curves.

paragraphs.context: Then she commanded the dogs to pick up speed again: “Get up!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack runs beside the sled. Annie tells the dogs to go faster, and they run up the hill and along the frozen shore.

paragraphs.context: Jack decided to keep running. It felt good to move in the biting cold.
paragraphs.simple: The team runs onto ice. The ice breaks under Jack, and his boots go into very cold water about 30 cm deep.

background.note: Along the coast, the trail sometimes crossed sea ice or frozen lagoons. Thin ice with water under it is very dangerous in the cold.

paragraphs.context: The team sailed ahead of Jack, pulling Annie and the sled away from the ice.
paragraphs.simple: The dogs pull Annie away. Jack tries to climb out, but more ice breaks. His feet get very wet.

paragraphs.context: “Stay back!” Jack shouted. “There’s thin ice here! Keep the dogs back!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie to keep the dogs away. Wet paws would freeze to the ice.

background.note: Sled dogs today often wear little cloth boots ("booties") to protect their pads from ice and snow.

paragraphs.context: As the dogs took off through the bone-chilling cold, Jack felt his feet burning with pain.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's feet hurt and then stop feeling. He knows wet feet lose heat 25 times faster than dry feet. He must get warm at once.

background.note: Frostbite happens when skin and the flesh under it freeze. Toes, fingers, ears and noses are most at risk. Bad frostbite can mean losing toes or fingers.

paragraphs.context: “We’ve come to a house!” yelled Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees a house with smoke from the chimney and a light inside. Jack can't see because of the ice on his glasses.

paragraphs.context: “Just in time!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Annie holds the sled with the snow hook, tells the dogs to stay, and helps Jack to the door of a log cabin.

paragraphs.context: A moment later, it opened. “Gunnar?” a man said, peering into the snowstorm.
paragraphs.simple: The man thinks they might be Gunnar. Annie says Jack's feet are wet, and the man tells them to come in.

paragraphs.context: With Annie’s help, Jack limped into the warm, firelit cabin.
paragraphs.simple: Jack walks in with Annie's help. The cabin is warm and lit by the fire.

paragraphs.context: Annie helped Jack pull off his fur boots and wool socks, then set them near the stove.
paragraphs.simple: They put Jack's boots and socks near the stove. The man pours hot water from a kettle into a bucket.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked at his wet feet. They were white and numb from the cold.
paragraphs.simple: His feet are white and have no feeling. He cannot move his toes.

paragraphs.context: As he put his feet into the warm water, he was overcome with pain.
paragraphs.simple: The warm water hurts his feet a lot. Jack wants to take them out, but the man says to keep them in.

background.note: Frozen skin should be warmed in warm (not hot) water. Warming it hurts a lot as the feeling comes back.

paragraphs.context: Listening to the howling wind and the snow pelting the cabin windows, he worried about the huskies.
paragraphs.simple: The wind howls and the snow hits the windows. Jack asks if the dogs can come in.

paragraphs.context: As Jack sat alone in the one-room cabin and soaked his feet, he worried about the time.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot find a clock. He wonders how long his boots will take to dry and if the dogs are hurt.

paragraphs.context: The man followed the team into the cabin and slammed the door against the storm.
paragraphs.simple: The tired, wet dogs walk slowly across the room and lie down in the straw.

paragraphs.context: “Ed’s a musher, too,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Ed is a musher and a mail carrier like Oki's uncle. He knows Uncle Joe's dogs.

background.note: The real Port Safety roadhouse was run by Ed Rohn, a musher who was supposed to take the medicine on the last part of the run.

paragraphs.context: Then Ed and Annie knelt in the straw and massaged the dogs’ feet, one paw at a time.
paragraphs.simple: Ed gives the dogs water. He and Annie rub each dog's feet. The dogs look as if they are smiling.

paragraphs.context: Jack saw that the musher was missing teeth and his beard was scraggly.
paragraphs.simple: Ed looks rough, but his face shows he is a strong, proud man. Jack respects him now that he understands a musher's work.

background.note: In 1925 mushers were paid to carry mail and goods. Mail teams pulled heavy sleds of letters and packages between towns all winter.

paragraphs.context: “Ed lives here, at the Port Safety roadhouse,” Annie said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie jokes that Port Safety is a good name for the place. Jack feels safe but worries about their twelve hours.

paragraphs.context: “Hold on.” Ed pulled out a pocket watch. “Almost midnight,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Ed looks at his watch. It is almost twelve o'clock at night.

background.note: In 1925 many men carried a watch on a chain in a pocket. Wristwatches became common later.

paragraphs.context: So almost eight and a half hours left to find Gunnar Kaasen and return to Nome, thought Jack.
paragraphs.simple: It is almost midnight. Jack asks why Ed called them Gunnar.

paragraphs.context: “I did mean Gunnar Kaasen,” said Ed.
paragraphs.simple: Ed was told to wait for Kaasen. If Kaasen is tired, Ed is to carry the medicine to Nome. Then he heard Kaasen would stay in Solomon.

background.term: take his package on to Nome
background.note: In the real relay, Kaasen was supposed to hand the medicine to Ed Rohn at Port Safety. But Kaasen arrived at about 3 a.m., found Rohn asleep, and decided to drive on to Nome himself.

paragraphs.context: “Good thing,” said Ed. “Only a crazy fool would drive in a storm like this.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ed asks why they were out.
paragraphs.simple: Ed says only a fool would drive in this storm, and asks why Jack and Annie were out.

paragraphs.context: “To exercise Oki’s uncle’s dogs,” said Jack, “while Oki’s at the hospital.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie say they took the dogs out for exercise and got lost.

paragraphs.context: “Good news,” said Ed.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's feet are pink and fine. Ed gives him a towel and big dry socks.

paragraphs.context: “You just dodged a case of frostbite, mister,” said Ed.
paragraphs.simple: Ed says Jack almost got frostbite. He thinks they will not go for a fun ride in a storm again.

paragraphs.context: “Well…um…they weren’t in Alaska,” Annie said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they won the "Frog Creek Winter Relay". Ed has never heard of it.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Annie has to invent a race quickly.

paragraphs.context: “Never heard of it,” said Ed. “Doesn’t matter.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ed will not let them go.
paragraphs.simple: Ed says they are not going out in the storm. The dogs need to rest and eat.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded. “Okay. But we have to keep our eye on the time.”
paragraphs.simple: They agree to stay a little longer, but they must watch the time.

paragraphs.context: The dogs gobbled up every piece of fish and drank from bowls of water.
paragraphs.simple: After eating, all eight dogs howl together, and the wind howls outside.

paragraphs.context: Jack knew the howling meant the dogs were satisfied.
paragraphs.simple: Howling means the dogs are happy. Then they suddenly stop.

paragraphs.context: The dogs then began nodding happily off to sleep, one by one.
paragraphs.simple: The dogs fall asleep. Some curl up and cover their noses with their tails.

background.term: covered their noses with their bushy tails
background.note: Huskies cover their noses with their tails to warm the air they breathe.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t know what to do.
paragraphs.simple: It is 1:15 a.m. They have only seven hours left to find Gunnar and get back.

paragraphs.context: “I’ll make some soup,” said Ed.
paragraphs.simple: Ed wants them to stay. He opens a can of tomato soup.

paragraphs.context: “It’s okay,” Annie whispered to Jack. “We have time.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they still have time. They wash their red, dry hands.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie smiled. They dried their hands and sat on two wooden barrels at the table.
paragraphs.simple: Ed gives them crackers, milk and hot soup while the storm is wild outside.

background.note: Soda crackers are dry, plain biscuits. They keep a long time, so people in far places kept them.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, thanks,” said Jack, sighing.
paragraphs.simple: The smell of the soup makes Jack forget his worries for a moment.

paragraphs.context: “Mmm, delicious!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie eat hot soup and crackers and watch the dogs sleep.

paragraphs.context: “Many do,” said Ed, resting in his armchair near the fire.
paragraphs.simple: Ed says that one day dogs will be used only for racing. Planes, cars, roads and snow machines will do the long trips.

background.term: vehicles that go through deep snow
background.note: Ed means snowmobiles. They were made in the 1960s, and soon replaced most working dog teams in Alaska.
In the 1930s small "bush planes" began carrying mail and medicine across Alaska.

paragraphs.context: “I’m with you, missy,” said Ed, looking at the sleeping dogs.
paragraphs.simple: Ed agrees with Annie. It makes him sad, because people have used sled dogs in Alaska for hundreds of years.
paragraphs.tone: Warm and a little sad. Ed calls himself an "old-timer": an old man who has lived there a long time.

paragraphs.context: “Sure do,” said Ed. “Balto is the best lead dog in Alaska, along with Togo, Leonhard Seppala’s dog.
paragraphs.simple: Ed says Balto and Togo are the best lead dogs in Alaska. Both have stopped at his roadhouse.

paragraphs.context: “Ahh, that dog loves to run a trail,” said Ed.
paragraphs.simple: Balto loves to run. He is big, black, strong and brave, and his spirit is beautiful to watch.

background.note: Balto was a black Siberian husky with a little white on his chest. Seppala owned him, but thought he was not good enough for his own team.

paragraphs.context: Ed smiled at her. “Alaskans are real respectful of animals, too,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Ed says Alaskans respect animals very much. They could not live without them.

paragraphs.context: “Well, the socks I just gave you are made of sheep’s wool,” said Ed.
paragraphs.simple: Their clothes are made from many animals. The medicine is wrapped in bear skin and is made from horse blood.

background.note: Reindeer were brought to Alaska from Siberia in the 1890s, partly to give food and skins to native Alaskans.
Caribou are wild North American reindeer. Native Alaskans used their meat, skins and bones.

paragraphs.context: “The blood of a horse,” said Ed. “It has antitoxins to kill diphtheria.”
paragraphs.simple: Serum comes from horse blood. It has antitoxins that fight diphtheria.

background.note: Horses were given small amounts of the diphtheria poison. Their blood then made antitoxin, which was taken out and used to treat sick people. The serum for Nome was 300,000 units in 20 pounds (about 9 kg) of glass bottles.

paragraphs.context: “Wow,” said Annie. “So Alaskans get gifts from”—she held up one finger after another—
paragraphs.simple: Annie counts all the animals on her fingers. Jack adds dogs.

paragraphs.context: “And fish and whales and birds of the air. All creatures,” said Ed.
paragraphs.simple: Ed says people, land, animals, sea and air all become one thing: Alaska.
paragraphs.tone: A quiet, deep thought about nature.

background.note: Native Alaskans on the coast hunted whales, seals and walruses for food, oil, skins and bones.

paragraphs.context: The three of them stared for a long moment at the dogs.
paragraphs.simple: Some dogs move their paws in their sleep, as if they are running in a dream.

paragraphs.context: Ed yawned, and his eyes started to close.
paragraphs.simple: Ed's head falls forward and he starts snoring.

paragraphs.context: Jack quietly put down his spoon.
paragraphs.simple: Jack quietly gets his dry boots and puts them on over Ed's big socks. He says they must go to Solomon to finish their job.

paragraphs.context: Ed snored loudly as Jack and Annie silently pulled on their fur parkas.
paragraphs.simple: They put on their coats and wake the dogs. The dogs make noise, but Ed keeps snoring.

background.note: "Parka" comes from a word used by native peoples of the far north and Russia. A real parka has a hood, often with fur around the face.

paragraphs.context: Outside, the wind and snow were blowing wildly.
paragraphs.simple: In the storm they take off their mittens just long enough to join the dogs to the lines.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man. I just thought of something,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers they should use the stardust so Ed will forget them.

paragraphs.context: Annie reached into her pocket and took out the dark blue box.
paragraphs.simple: The stardust shines like starlight. Annie throws it in the air and wishes for them to be forgotten.

paragraphs.context: The stardust flashed through the room, then quickly evaporated.
paragraphs.simple: The bowls are clean, Jack's wet socks are gone, the soup can is back on the shelf, and the hay is neat again.

background.note: Things that evaporate turn from liquid into gas and disappear. Here the magic dust just disappears.

paragraphs.context: “Except Ed will be missing a pair of his socks,” whispered Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Only one sign is left: Jack is still wearing Ed's socks.

paragraphs.context: Jack stood on the sled runners, crouching slightly and gripping the handlebars.
paragraphs.simple: Jack holds the handles. The dogs bark as if they say YES.

paragraphs.context: The eight huskies surged forward.
paragraphs.simple: The dogs run fast away from Port Safety into the storm.

paragraphs.context: As the basket bounced and bumped over uneven ridges on the trail,
paragraphs.simple: Annie almost falls out, but she laughs and enjoys it.

paragraphs.context: The wind from the frozen sea was bitterly cold.
paragraphs.simple: The wind is very cold. The dogs keep their heads down and run on and on.

paragraphs.context: Jack used his skills to move the team around banks of drifting snow.
paragraphs.simple: Jack steers around piles of snow. Strong winds blow as they travel along the edge of the sea.

background.note: A gale is a wind of about 62–88 km/h (39–54 mph).

paragraphs.context: Like sand in a sandstorm, ice crystals beat against his face, stinging his skin.
paragraphs.simple: Ice hits his face and hurts. His fur clothes keep him safe, and he thanks the animals that gave them.

background.note: In great cold, blowing snow is made of tiny hard ice crystals that feel like sand.

paragraphs.context: Before he could give a command to stop the dogs, a fierce gust of wind slammed against the sled,
paragraphs.simple: A strong wind pushes the sled into a pile of snow. Jack falls into the snow.

paragraphs.context: “Here! Here!” said Jack, floundering as he tried to get up.
paragraphs.simple: His heavy clothes make it hard to stand. Annie helps him up.

paragraphs.context: The dogs straightened their lines.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is ready to drive, but she tells Jack to listen.

paragraphs.context: “Bells! I hear bells!” Annie shouted. “Up ahead!”
paragraphs.simple: They hear bells. Another dog team is coming. Maybe it is Gunnar and Balto.

paragraphs.context: But the sound of the bells stopped suddenly.
paragraphs.simple: The bells stop, and dogs bark in a scared, high way.
paragraphs.tone: A cliffhanger: the chapter ends at an exciting moment.

paragraphs.context: Annie drove the huskies through the dark toward the frantic barking.
paragraphs.simple: They find another team in deep snow. The sled has turned over. The driver is trying to free his dogs.

paragraphs.context: “Whoa!” Annie ordered. “Stay!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie stops the team. Jack fixes the snow hook in the ground. They walk slowly through the strong wind.

background.note: A snow hook is a heavy metal hook that a musher pushes into the snow to keep the team from running off.

paragraphs.context: “Yes! Just hit a bump back there!” said the famous dog musher.
paragraphs.simple: The driver is Gunnar Kaasen. His sled hit a bump, flew up and fell on its side.

paragraphs.context: Annie and Jack began helping Gunnar.
paragraphs.simple: They pull the dogs out of the soft snow one by one. There are thirteen dogs.

background.note: Kaasen's real team had 13 dogs, led by Balto. Kaasen drove them 53 miles (85 km) through the storm in the dark.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie helped Gunnar turn the sled upright, setting it back on its runners.
paragraphs.simple: They turn the sled right side up and press down the snow so the dogs can pull it out.

paragraphs.context: Soon the dogs were lined up in pairs in front of the sled, with a single dog in the lead.
paragraphs.simple: One dog runs alone in front. It is Balto. He jumps up and licks Annie's face.

paragraphs.context: “Yes!” the musher said, leaning over the sled.
paragraphs.simple: Gunnar looks for the medicine, but the package is missing.

paragraphs.context: “It was tied to the sled!” shouted Gunnar.
paragraphs.simple: The package fell off the sled. Gunnar falls to his knees and digs wildly in the snow.

background.note: This really happened: Kaasen's sled turned over in the storm, and the serum fell into the snow. He found it by digging with his bare hands, and his fingers got frostbite.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, wait!” said Annie. “I’ll bet Balto can find it!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks Balto can find the package. She takes him off the line. Jack is afraid they will lose Balto too.

paragraphs.context: She grabbed the lead dog’s head between her mittens and put her face close to his,
paragraphs.simple: Annie holds Balto's head and whispers to him. Then she lets him go to find the medicine.

paragraphs.context: While Gunnar crawled around in the snow looking for the package,
paragraphs.simple: Balto goes back along the trail with his nose to the ground.

background.note: Dogs can smell about 10,000 to 100,000 times better than people.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt around in the windswept snow until he touched something soft and solid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a heavy bag wrapped in fur. Balto found it.

background.note: The real serum package weighed about 20 pounds (9 kg). It was wrapped in quilts and canvas to keep it from freezing.

paragraphs.context: “Gunnar!” Jack yelled. “We found the package!”
paragraphs.simple: The wind is too loud for Gunnar to hear. They carry the package back with Balto.

paragraphs.context: When they reached Gunnar’s team, Annie quickly hooked Balto to the front of the line.
paragraphs.simple: Annie puts Balto back in front. Gunnar is still digging in the snow with his hands.

paragraphs.context: Gunnar gave a happy shout and staggered to his feet.
paragraphs.simple: Gunnar shouts with joy. Jack gives him the package, and he ties it tightly to his sled.

paragraphs.context: “Thank you!” shouted Gunnar Kaasen. “I won’t forget you! Thank you!”
paragraphs.simple: Gunnar says he will not forget them. (But the stardust will make him forget.)
paragraphs.tone: A little ironic: the reader knows the magic will make people forget them.

paragraphs.context: As he climbed into the basket, Jack thought about the Port Safety roadhouse.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks it would be strange to meet Ed again, because Ed will not remember them.

paragraphs.context: Annie stood on the runners and waited.
paragraphs.simple: Gunnar's 13 dogs run past with Balto in front. Annie's team follows them.

paragraphs.context: “Jack, look! Gunnar kept going!” yelled Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Gunnar does not stop at Port Safety. He keeps going to Nome.

background.term: He didn’t stop at the roadhouse
background.note: In real life, Ed Rohn was asleep, and Kaasen thought waking him and changing teams would waste time, so he drove on to Nome.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie’s huskies kept following the jingling bells of Balto
paragraphs.simple: Their dogs seem stronger than before. It is as if Balto is leading both teams.

background.note: The last part of the trail went along the coast of the Bering Sea from Solomon to Nome.

paragraphs.context: Guided by Balto’s spirit, all twenty-one dogs flew over the flat shoreline.
paragraphs.simple: All 21 dogs run very fast. The snow and wind stop, and the sky starts to clear.

paragraphs.context: In the early gray dawn, Jack saw a church steeple in the distance.
paragraphs.simple: At dawn Jack sees a church tower and lights in houses. They are back in Nome.

background.note: Kaasen and Balto reached Nome at about 5:30 a.m. on February 2, 1925.

paragraphs.context: “Haw!” commanded Annie. And the dogs veered left
paragraphs.simple: Annie turns the dogs left toward Uncle Joe's shack.

paragraphs.context: In the early light, the huskies stopped at Uncle Joe’s shack.
paragraphs.simple: Oki runs out, and his uncle follows on his crutch. The tired dogs jump and bark with joy.

paragraphs.context: Jack climbed out of the sled as Annie stepped off the runners.
paragraphs.simple: Their faces and clothes are covered with thin ice, but they laugh and move their feet and arms to get warm.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled at Annie. “With time to spare!” he said.
paragraphs.simple: It is almost six o'clock, so they are back before their magic ends at 8:30.

paragraphs.context: “We did!” said Annie. “On the trail below Port Safety!
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells how Gunnar's sled turned over and Balto helped find the medicine. Gunnar is taking it to the hospital.

paragraphs.context: Uncle Joe closed his eyes and sighed with relief. Oki couldn’t stop grinning.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Joe is very relieved. Oki shakes their hands hard and calls them champions.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t thank us!” said Jack. “Thank your dogs—they’re the real champions!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the dogs are the true champions.

paragraphs.context: Oki opened the gate to the dog pen.
paragraphs.simple: They take the harnesses off the tired dogs and rub their backs and legs.

paragraphs.context: Oki gave the dogs water, and Jack and Annie fed them dried fish.
paragraphs.simple: The dogs eat fast and howl with thanks. Then they curl up in the snow and sleep.

background.note: Huskies often howl together, like wolves. They howl to talk to each other and when they are excited.

paragraphs.context: Uncle Joe hobbled on his crutch as the four of them headed to town.
paragraphs.simple: They walk to town. The early-morning sky is bright blue, and the snow looks blue too. This is the "blue dawn" of the book's title.

paragraphs.context: By the time they arrived at the hospital, a small crowd had gathered.
paragraphs.simple: A crowd waits at the hospital. Reporters with cameras talk to Mayor Maynard and Gunnar Kaasen.

background.note: The serum run was big news. Newspapers and radio across the U.S. followed it every day, and Balto became a star. He even appeared in a short movie in 1925.

paragraphs.context: Gunnar’s huskies were off to the side.
paragraphs.simple: Children pet Gunnar's dogs, and photographers take pictures.

paragraphs.context: “The newspapers are here!” said Oki.
paragraphs.simple: Oki says the whole world will hear the story, and Jack and Annie will be honored too.

paragraphs.context: “Whoa, wait,” Jack said to Annie. “Stardust.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers that nobody must know about them. Annie takes out the blue box.

paragraphs.context: As Oki and his uncle headed toward the crowd, Annie lifted the lid of the tiny box.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wishes that everyone who saw them will forget them. She throws the stardust in the air.

paragraphs.context: Like tiny grains of windswept snow, the stardust flashed brilliantly over the street.
paragraphs.simple: The dust shines brightly and then disappears before anyone looks up.

paragraphs.context: Then she and Jack headed toward the gathering in front of the hospital.
paragraphs.simple: Oki, his uncle and Gunnar look at Jack and Annie but do not know them.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, no one remembers us at all,” Annie said. She sounded sad.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie feel a little sad that nobody remembers them.
paragraphs.tone: Bittersweet: happy that they helped, sad that they are forgotten.

paragraphs.context: Mayor Maynard proudly stepped forward.
paragraphs.simple: The mayor says 20 mushers and over 160 dogs carried the medicine to Nome in five and a half days.

background.note: The run took about 127½ hours. It began on January 27 in Nenana and ended on February 2, 1925, in Nome.

paragraphs.context: “Nearly seven hundred miles!” said the mayor.
paragraphs.simple: The relay went almost 700 miles. Seppala and Togo crossed the frozen Norton Sound, and Kaasen and Balto ran from Bluff to Nome.

background.note: Norton Sound is a big bay of the Bering Sea. Seppala took a shortcut across its ice, which saved a day but was very dangerous.
Bluff was a small mining camp. Kaasen took the serum there from Charlie Olson and ran the last 53 miles to Nome.
The radio in chapter 3 said "six hundred miles". The real distance from Nenana to Nome is about 674 miles (1,085 km).

paragraphs.context: “I owe everything to my lead dog, Balto!” said Gunnar.
paragraphs.simple: Gunnar says he owes everything to Balto. Balto sits quietly nearby.

background.term: I owe everything to my lead dog, Balto!
background.note: Kaasen later said Balto found the trail in the storm when he himself could not see it.

paragraphs.context: In the daylight, Jack got a good look at Balto.
paragraphs.simple: Balto has shaggy black fur, white paws, a white chest and gentle brown eyes.

background.note: Balto was a working sled dog, not a show dog. After his death his body was preserved, and it is now at a museum in Cleveland, Ohio.

paragraphs.context: “I…well, I…” The musher shook his head. “I’m not sure.

paragraphs.context: “It seems like a miracle!” the reporter said.
paragraphs.simple: The reporter says finding it was like a miracle. Losing it would have been a disaster.

paragraphs.context: “Indeed,” said Mayor Maynard.
paragraphs.simple: The mayor says all the work would have been wasted if the medicine was lost. He has given it to Dr. Welch and Nurse Morgan.

background.term: give the lifesaving serum to their patients
background.note: The serum stopped the epidemic. Officially about five or six people died, though more native Alaskan deaths may not have been counted.

paragraphs.context: The reporter was asking more questions as Jack and Annie pulled away from the crowd,
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie walk away toward the tree house. Then they hear barking.

paragraphs.context: “Balto!” said Annie. She knelt in the blue dawn and reached out her arms.
paragraphs.simple: Balto runs to Annie and licks her face. His eyes shine. He seems to smile.

paragraphs.context: “He remembers us, Jack!” said Annie. “Balto remembers us!”
paragraphs.simple: The magic did not work on Balto. Jack jokes that it is okay because Balto won't tell anyone.

paragraphs.context: “Go on, Balto,” Annie said. “You’re their hero. They need you.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Balto to go back to the people who need him.

paragraphs.context: Balto gave her one more lick.
paragraphs.simple: Balto runs back proudly to the crowd. Sunlight shines on the edges of his fur.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie turned away and headed down the boardwalk.
paragraphs.simple: They walk back along the creek, over the bridge and across the frozen field to the tree house.

paragraphs.context: In his thick fur boots and mittens, Jack clumsily climbed the rope ladder.
paragraphs.simple: From the window, the sunlight on the snow and ice is so bright that they can hardly see.

background.note: Snow reflects most sunlight. In the far north people wore snow goggles with thin slits to stop snow blindness.

paragraphs.context: “Yep,” said Annie. “Now let’s go home and get warm.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie points to a picture of the Frog Creek woods and wishes to go home.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt warm, wonderfully warm.
paragraphs.simple: They are in summer clothes again. No time has passed at home. It is still evening.

background.term: No time at all had passed
background.note: In every Magic Tree House book, no time passes at home while Jack and Annie are away.

paragraphs.context: “Really nice,” said Jack. He reached into his pocket and took out the tiny box, empty of gold dust now.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie put the empty boxes on the floor next to the Alaska guide.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, a little cold, a little stressful,” said Jack, “but all in all, very good.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the trip was cold and worrying, but good. Annie says the dogs were the best part.

paragraphs.context: “And really smart, too. Like Saint Bernards. Remember Barry in Switzerland?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers Barry, a Saint Bernard puppy, from another mission in Switzerland.

background.note: In Magic Tree House #46, Dogs in the Dead of Night, Jack and Annie meet Barry, a famous Saint Bernard rescue dog in the Swiss Alps.

paragraphs.context: “And remember when Morgan turned Teddy into a terrier?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers when Teddy was a little dog (a terrier) because of a spell.

background.note: In Magic Tree House #17–20 Teddy was a little terrier because of a spell. Jack and Annie's kindness set him free.

paragraphs.context: “Of course,” Jack said. “We’d better walk our bikes now. It’s getting dark fast.”
paragraphs.simple: It is getting dark, so they push their bikes through the woods.

paragraphs.context: The woods were filled with the sounds of summer.
paragraphs.simple: Frogs, crickets and an owl make summer sounds. Then they hear a small dog: Yip!

background.note: Bullfrogs are big North American frogs. Their deep call sounds a little like a cow.

paragraphs.context: “No way,” said Jack. “That’s too much of a coincidence!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks a dog here, after a dog mission, would be too surprising.

paragraphs.context: In the dark, Annie got down on her hands and knees.
paragraphs.simple: Annie looks in the leaves and finds a little black-and-white puppy.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached out, and the next thing he knew, his hand was wet from puppy licks.
paragraphs.simple: The puppy licks Jack's hand. Jack laughs.

paragraphs.context: Jack tried to steer two bikes through the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Annie runs ahead with the puppy. Jack pushes both bikes to the sidewalk.

paragraphs.context: “Let me see him,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Under the street light, the puppy has big brown eyes and soft, curly black-and-white fur.

background.note: Oki the puppy appears on the covers of later Magic Tree House books.

paragraphs.context: “Lots of dogs! All sizes, big, small, and in between.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the puppy is a mix of all the dogs they have loved. This links back to her wish in chapter 1 for big, small and "in-between" dogs.

paragraphs.context: “They will,” said Annie. “They said we could get a dog when we found the right one.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is sure their parents will let them keep him. If he is lost, they will ask people and put up signs.

paragraphs.context: “But I have a feeling he’s not lost. I think he was actually in the woods waiting for us.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the puppy is a thank-you gift from Merlin and Morgan.

paragraphs.context: “Hmm…” Annie thought for a moment. “What about Oki?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to name him Oki, after the boy. Jack agrees.

background.note: From this book on, the puppy Oki becomes Jack and Annie's dog in the series.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah…,” said Jack. “But, hey, just promise me
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks Annie never to say "Okey dokey, Oki".

paragraphs.context: “Okey dokey, Oki,” said Annie. “Let’s go inside.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the words Jack asked her not to say.
paragraphs.tone: A funny ending: Annie breaks her promise at once.

paragraphs.context: For more than one hundred years, sled dog racing has been a favorite sport in Alaska.
paragraphs.simple: In 1925 a relay of dog teams carried diphtheria medicine to Nome in less than six days. It was called the Great Race of Mercy.

background.note: Anchorage is Alaska's biggest city. In 1925 the serum went by train from Anchorage to Nenana, and then by dog sled to Nome.

paragraphs.context: Many brave mushers and their dogs risked their lives in brutal weather
paragraphs.simple: The story was told across the country. It helped people understand that vaccines can stop diseases.

paragraphs.context: Most famous of the dogsled drivers was Leonhard Seppala,
paragraphs.simple: Seppala and Togo carried the medicine the longest way. But Kaasen and Balto got the most praise because they arrived in Nome.

background.note: Balto got most of the fame. Many mushers felt Togo, who ran about 260 miles of the relay, deserved more.

paragraphs.context: There was some controversy surrounding the fact that Kaasen received so much credit,
paragraphs.simple: Some people said Kaasen should have stopped at Port Safety for Ed Rohn. Kaasen said the cabin was dark, so he did not want to waste time.

background.note: Ed Rohn was waiting at Port Safety with a fresh team. He was asleep when Kaasen came by at about 3 a.m.

paragraphs.context: Regardless of the debate over who should have received the most credit,
paragraphs.simple: Whoever got the most praise, the race showed the courage, strength and skill of all the mushers and dogs.

paragraphs.context: Today people remember the serum race every spring,
paragraphs.simple: Today the Iditarod race remembers the serum run every year.

background.note: The Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race began in 1973. It runs about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) from Anchorage to Nome every March.
