parts.meaning: In the bright light of the moon,
Jack could see

parts.text: that the shack was made of old driftwood
parts.meaning: that the hut was built from old wood carried by the sea
and metal cans that were pressed flat.

sentences.grammar: "Be made of" tells the material. "Flattened" is a past participle used as an adjective.

sentences.context: Eight huskies were sleeping in the snow, their dark bodies curled up together to keep warm.
sentences.simple: Eight huskies were sleeping in the snow. Their dark bodies were curled up close together so they stayed warm.
sentences.main: Eight huskies were sleeping in the snow.

parts.text: Eight huskies were sleeping in the snow,
parts.meaning: Eight huskies were sleeping in the snow,

parts.text: their dark bodies curled up together
parts.meaning: with their dark bodies curled up close to each other
so that they could stay warm.

sentences.grammar: The part "their dark bodies curled up together" has no verb "were": it is an absolute phrase that adds a picture to the main part.

sentences.context: Twenty of the best mushers and more than a hundred and sixty dogs have been heroically running a relay across the frozen tundra.
sentences.simple: Twenty of the best dog drivers and more than 160 dogs have been bravely carrying the medicine, team after team, across the frozen land.
sentences.main: Mushers and dogs have been running a relay.

parts.meaning: Twenty of the best dog sled drivers

parts.text: and more than a hundred and sixty dogs
parts.meaning: and over 160 dogs

parts.text: have been heroically running a relay
parts.meaning: have been bravely running a race in parts
across the frozen, flat, treeless land.

sentences.grammar: "Have been running" is present perfect continuous: it started before and is still going on now.

sentences.context: He barely glanced at Jack and Annie as he fixed his gaze on Oki.
sentences.simple: He almost did not look at Jack and Annie, because he looked hard only at Oki.
sentences.main: He barely glanced at Jack and Annie.

parts.text: He barely glanced at Jack and Annie
parts.meaning: He looked very quickly at Jack and Annie, almost not at all,

parts.text: as he fixed his gaze on Oki.
parts.meaning: while he kept looking at Oki.

sentences.grammar: "Barely" = almost not. "As" here means "while; at the same time". "Fix your gaze on" = look steadily at.

sentences.context: “If he waits, he waits for good reason,” said Oki’s uncle.
sentences.simple: Oki's uncle said: if Kaasen is waiting, there is a good reason for it.
sentences.main: He waits for good reason.

parts.meaning: If he waits,
there is a good reason why he waits,
said Oki's uncle.

sentences.grammar: A zero conditional: "If + present, present" talks about something that is generally true.

sentences.context: Who will help you if the ice breaks and moves out to sea?
sentences.simple: Who will help you if the ice cracks and floats away into the sea?
sentences.main: Who will help you?

parts.meaning: Who will help you

parts.text: if the ice breaks and moves out to sea?
parts.meaning: if the ice breaks and floats away into the sea?

sentences.grammar: A first conditional question: "Who will...if + present?" "Out to sea" = away from land, into the sea.

sentences.context: He was a little nervous about losing their way and freezing to death, but he nodded again.
sentences.simple: He was a bit afraid that they might get lost and die from the cold, but he nodded again.
sentences.main: He was a little nervous, but he nodded again.

parts.meaning: He was a bit worried

parts.text: about losing their way and freezing to death,
parts.meaning: about getting lost and dying of cold,
but he moved his head to say yes again.

sentences.grammar: "Nervous about + -ing". "Lose your way" = get lost.

sentences.context: I lost my wife and my two children seven years ago in the flu epidemic.
sentences.simple: My wife and my two children died seven years ago when the flu spread through the town.
sentences.main: I lost my wife and my two children.

parts.text: I lost my wife and my two children
parts.meaning: My wife and my two children died
seven years ago
when the flu made many people sick.

sentences.grammar: "Lose someone" can mean that someone close to you died. Seven years before 1925 is 1918, the year of the great flu epidemic.

sentences.context: They have traveled the trail hundreds of times, delivering mail with me.
sentences.simple: They have run on the trail hundreds of times, bringing mail with me.
sentences.main: They have traveled the trail hundreds of times.

parts.meaning: They have run along the trail
many hundreds of times,
carrying letters with me.

sentences.grammar: "Have traveled" is present perfect: experience up to now. The -ing phrase tells what they were doing.

sentences.context: He knew not to scold the dogs and risk dampening their enthusiasm.
sentences.simple: He knew that he should not shout at the dogs, because that might make them less excited to run.
sentences.main: He knew not to scold the dogs.

parts.text: He knew not to scold the dogs
parts.meaning: He knew he should not speak angrily to the dogs
and maybe make them less eager.

sentences.grammar: "Know not to + verb" = know that you should not do it. "Risk + -ing" = do something that might cause a bad result.

sentences.context: He gripped the two handles of the sled, bent his knees, and leaned forward.
sentences.simple: He held the two handles of the sled tightly, bent his knees and leaned forward.
sentences.main: He gripped the handles, bent his knees, and leaned forward.

parts.text: He gripped the two handles of the sled,
parts.meaning: He held the two handles of the sled tightly,
bent his knees,
and moved his body forward.

sentences.grammar: A list of three past actions with one subject. "Bent" is the past form of "bend".

sentences.context: He knew how to push in the perfect rhythm to keep the team from running too fast, so they wouldn’t pant and hurt their lungs in the freezing air.
sentences.simple: He knew how to push at exactly the right speed so the dogs did not run too fast. Then they would not breathe too hard and hurt their lungs in the very cold air.
sentences.main: He knew how to push in the perfect rhythm.

parts.text: He knew how to push in the perfect rhythm
parts.meaning: He knew how to push at exactly the right beat

parts.text: to keep the team from running too fast,
parts.meaning: so the dogs would not run too fast,

parts.text: so they wouldn’t pant and hurt their lungs
parts.meaning: so they would not breathe hard and damage their lungs
in the very cold air.

sentences.grammar: "Keep someone from + -ing" = stop them doing it. "So" here means "so that; with this result".

sentences.context: He knew the fewer words, the better.
sentences.simple: He knew that using fewer words was better.
sentences.main: The fewer words, the better.

parts.meaning: He knew
using fewer words is better.

sentences.grammar: "The + comparative ..., the + comparative" shows that two things change together: "the fewer words, the better" = fewer words are better.

sentences.context: When they labored up an incline, he lightened their load by hopping off and running beside the sled, holding on to one of the handles to keep it steady.
sentences.simple: When the dogs worked hard to go up a hill, he made the sled lighter: he jumped off and ran next to it, holding a handle so it stayed steady.
sentences.main: He lightened their load.

parts.text: When they labored up an incline,
parts.meaning: When the dogs pulled hard up a hill,
he made their load lighter

parts.text: by hopping off and running beside the sled,
parts.meaning: by jumping off and running next to the sled,

parts.text: holding on to one of the handles
parts.meaning: while holding one of the handles
so that it did not shake.

sentences.grammar: "By + -ing" tells how. "Keep + object + adjective" = make it stay that way: "keep it steady".

sentences.context: Lost in his thoughts, Jack failed to notice a change in the weather, until he heard Annie call out, “The storm’s starting!”
sentences.simple: Jack was thinking so much that he did not notice the weather change, until Annie shouted that the storm was starting.
sentences.main: Jack failed to notice a change in the weather.

parts.meaning: Because he was thinking hard,

parts.text: Jack failed to notice a change in the weather,
parts.meaning: Jack did not see that the weather was changing,

parts.text: until he heard Annie call out,
parts.meaning: until he heard Annie shout,
"The storm is starting!"

sentences.grammar: "Fail to + verb" = not do it. "Hear someone + verb" (no "to"): "heard Annie call out".

sentences.context: Flying blindly down the trail, he tried to wipe his glasses with a fur mitten, but that only made it worse.
sentences.simple: While moving very fast down the trail without seeing, he tried to clean his glasses with his fur glove, but that made it worse.
sentences.main: He tried to wipe his glasses.

parts.meaning: Going very fast down the trail without being able to see,

parts.text: he tried to wipe his glasses with a fur mitten,
parts.meaning: he tried to clean his glasses with a fur glove,

parts.text: but that only made it worse.
parts.meaning: but that just made the problem bigger.

sentences.grammar: The -ing phrase at the start ("Flying blindly...") happens at the same time as the main verb. "Make it worse" = make it more bad.

sentences.context: She never let the towline go slack and get tangled with the other lines.
sentences.simple: She never allowed the main rope to become loose and twist together with the other ropes.
sentences.main: She never let the towline go slack.

parts.meaning: She never allowed the main rope
to become loose

parts.text: and get tangled with the other lines.
parts.meaning: and get twisted together with the other ropes.

sentences.grammar: "Let + object + verb" (no "to"). "Go slack", "get tangled": "go" and "get" mean "become" here.

sentences.context: If the huskies got their feet wet, their soft pads would quickly stick to the ice and freeze.
sentences.simple: If the dogs' feet got wet, the soft parts under their feet would soon stick to the ice and freeze.
sentences.main: Their soft pads would stick to the ice and freeze.

parts.text: If the huskies got their feet wet,
parts.meaning: If the dogs' feet became wet,

parts.text: their soft pads would quickly stick to the ice
parts.meaning: the soft bottoms of their feet would soon stick to the ice
and freeze.

sentences.grammar: A second conditional: "If + past, ... would + verb" talks about something that might happen. "Get + object + adjective" = make it that way: "got their feet wet".

sentences.context: As an expert musher, he knew that wet feet lost heat twenty-five times faster than dry feet.
sentences.simple: Because he was an expert dog sled driver, he knew that wet feet get cold 25 times faster than dry feet.
sentences.main: He knew that wet feet lost heat faster.

parts.meaning: Because he was a very skilled musher,
he knew
that wet feet lose warmth

parts.text: twenty-five times faster than dry feet.
parts.meaning: 25 times more quickly than dry feet.

sentences.grammar: "As + noun" = in the role of. "X times faster than" compares speeds. After "knew", the verb moves to the past ("lost"), even for a general fact.

sentences.context: How long would it take for his boots to dry? he wondered.
sentences.simple: He asked himself how much time his boots needed to get dry.
sentences.main: How long would it take for his boots to dry?

parts.meaning: How much time would be needed
for his boots to become dry?
he asked himself.

sentences.grammar: "It takes + time + for something + to + verb". The question shows Jack's thoughts.

sentences.context: Now that he understood the job of a professional musher, he admired Ed a lot.
sentences.simple: Because he now knew what a real musher's job was like, he respected Ed very much.
sentences.main: He admired Ed a lot.

parts.text: Now that he understood the job of a professional musher,
parts.meaning: Because he now knew the work of a real musher,
he respected Ed very much.

sentences.grammar: "Now that" = because now. "Admire" = respect and like.

sentences.context: If he gets tired on his journey, I’m supposed to take his package on to Nome.
sentences.simple: If he is tired, my job is to carry his package the rest of the way to Nome.
sentences.main: I'm supposed to take his package on to Nome.

parts.text: If he gets tired on his journey,
parts.meaning: If he becomes tired on his trip,

parts.text: I’m supposed to take his package
parts.meaning: I should carry his package
farther, all the way to Nome.

sentences.grammar: "Be supposed to" = be expected to, because someone told you. "On" here means "farther; continuing".

sentences.context: These socks will be too big, but better big socks than wet ones.
sentences.simple: These socks are too big for you, but big socks are better than wet socks.
sentences.main: Better big socks than wet ones.

parts.text: These socks will be too big,
parts.meaning: These socks will be too large for you,

parts.text: but better big socks than wet ones.
parts.meaning: but big socks are better than wet socks.

sentences.grammar: "Better A than B" is a short way to say "A is better than B". "Ones" stands for "socks", so we do not repeat the noun.

sentences.context: The wind howled outside as all eight dogs howled inside.
sentences.simple: The wind made a long loud sound outside while the eight dogs made the same sound inside.
sentences.main: The wind howled outside.

parts.meaning: The wind made a long, loud noise outside

parts.text: as all eight dogs howled inside.
parts.meaning: while all eight dogs howled inside.

sentences.grammar: "As" here means "while; at the same time". The writer repeats "howled" to make a picture.

sentences.context: He seemed determined to keep them from going back out into the blizzard.
sentences.simple: He clearly wanted to stop them from going back out into the snowstorm.
sentences.main: He seemed determined to keep them from going.

parts.meaning: He seemed to have decided strongly

parts.text: to keep them from going back out
parts.meaning: to stop them from going outside again
into the bad snowstorm.

sentences.grammar: "Determined to + verb" = having firmly decided to do it. "Keep someone from + -ing" = stop them doing it.

sentences.context: But the day is coming when dogs won’t be used much anymore, except for racing.
sentences.simple: But soon there will be a time when people do not use dogs much, only for races.
sentences.main: The day is coming.

parts.meaning: But a time will soon come

parts.text: when dogs won’t be used much anymore,
parts.meaning: when people will not use dogs very much,
only for races.

sentences.grammar: "Won't be used" is future passive. "When" begins a clause that describes "the day".

sentences.context: People here have learned to use all the gifts this frozen world can give.
sentences.simple: People in Alaska have learned to use everything useful that this cold land gives them.
sentences.main: People here have learned to use all the gifts.

parts.meaning: People here have learned
to use all the good things
that this cold world can give.

sentences.grammar: "The gifts (that) this frozen world can give": "that" is left out before a clause that describes a noun.

sentences.context: The medicine headed for Nome is wrapped in bear hide.
sentences.simple: The medicine that is going to Nome is wrapped in bear skin.
sentences.main: The medicine is wrapped in bear hide.

parts.meaning: The medicine that is going to Nome
is covered in the skin of a bear.

sentences.grammar: "Headed for Nome" is a short form of "that is headed for Nome". "Is wrapped" is passive.

sentences.context: So he pulled the boots over the big pair of socks Ed had given him.
sentences.simple: So he put the boots on over the big socks that Ed gave him.
sentences.main: He pulled the boots over the big pair of socks.

parts.meaning: So he pulled on the boots

parts.text: over the big pair of socks
parts.meaning: over the big socks
that Ed had given him.

sentences.grammar: "Had given" is past perfect: Ed gave them earlier. "That" is left out before "Ed had given him".

sentences.context: He was grateful to all the creatures that had given their gifts to help Alaskans survive in their frozen world.
sentences.simple: He felt thankful to all the animals whose skins and fur helped Alaskans stay alive in their cold land.
sentences.main: He was grateful to all the creatures.

parts.text: He was grateful to all the creatures
parts.meaning: He felt thankful to all the animals
that had given things

parts.text: to help Alaskans survive in their frozen world.
parts.meaning: to help Alaskans live in their very cold land.

sentences.grammar: "Had given" is past perfect: it happened before the time of the story. "Help + someone + verb" (no "to").

sentences.context: Before he could give a command to stop the dogs, a fierce gust of wind slammed against the sled, sending it into a bank.
sentences.simple: A very strong wind hit the sled before he could tell the dogs to stop, and pushed it into a pile of snow.
sentences.main: A fierce gust of wind slammed against the sled.

parts.text: Before he could give a command to stop the dogs,
parts.meaning: Before he was able to tell the dogs to stop,

parts.text: a fierce gust of wind slammed against the sled,
parts.meaning: a very strong blow of wind hit the sled hard,
and pushed it into a pile of snow.

sentences.grammar: The -ing phrase "sending it into a bank" shows the result of the main action.

sentences.context: By the time the dogs were all on their feet again, Jack had counted thirteen huskies.
sentences.simple: When all the dogs were standing again, Jack had counted thirteen huskies.
sentences.main: Jack had counted thirteen huskies.

parts.text: By the time the dogs were all on their feet again,
parts.meaning: When the dogs were all standing up again,
Jack had counted 13 huskies.

sentences.grammar: "By the time + past, ... had + past participle": the second action was finished before or at that time.

sentences.context: In the biting wind, the musher fell to his knees and frantically dug through the snow, looking for the medicine package.
sentences.simple: In the very cold wind, the musher dropped onto his knees and dug wildly in the snow to find the medicine.
sentences.main: The musher fell to his knees and dug through the snow.

parts.meaning: In the very cold, painful wind,

parts.text: the musher fell to his knees
parts.meaning: the musher dropped down onto his knees

parts.text: and frantically dug through the snow,
parts.meaning: and dug in the snow in a very worried way,
trying to find the medicine package.

sentences.grammar: "Dug" is the past form of "dig". The -ing phrase "looking for..." tells what he was trying to do.

sentences.context: With his nose to the ground, the husky trotted back down the trail.
sentences.simple: The husky ran back along the trail at a medium speed, smelling the ground.
sentences.main: The husky trotted back down the trail.

parts.text: With his nose to the ground,
parts.meaning: Smelling the ground,

parts.text: the husky trotted back down the trail.
parts.meaning: the husky ran back along the trail.

sentences.grammar: "With + noun + phrase" describes how someone does something: "with his nose to the ground".

sentences.context: It would be weird to meet Ed all over again, as if for the first time.
sentences.simple: It would be strange to meet Ed again and act as if they had never met.
sentences.main: It would be weird to meet Ed all over again.

parts.meaning: It would be strange

parts.text: to meet Ed all over again,
parts.meaning: to meet Ed once more,

parts.text: as if for the first time.
parts.meaning: like it was the first time.

sentences.grammar: "It would be + adjective + to + verb": "it" stands for the "to" part. "As if for the first time" is short for "as if it were for the first time".

sentences.context: It was as if Balto was leading their team as well as his own.
sentences.simple: It seemed that Balto was leading their team and also his own team.
sentences.main: Balto was leading their team as well as his own.

parts.meaning: It seemed that
Balto was leading Jack and Annie's team
and also his own team.

sentences.grammar: "As if" says how something seems. "His own" = his own team; the noun is left out.

sentences.context: Though exhausted, the dogs had enough energy to jump up and down and bark excitedly as their two friends greeted them with great joy.
sentences.simple: The dogs were very tired, but they still had enough energy to jump and bark happily when their two friends said hello to them.
sentences.main: The dogs had enough energy to jump and bark.

parts.meaning: Even though they were very tired,
the dogs had enough strength

parts.text: to jump up and down and bark excitedly
parts.meaning: to jump up and down and bark with excitement

parts.text: as their two friends greeted them with great joy.
parts.meaning: when their two friends said hello very happily.

sentences.grammar: "Though exhausted" is short for "though they were exhausted". "Enough + noun + to + verb".

sentences.context: Reflecting the brilliant blue of the early-morning sky, the snow itself looked blue.
sentences.simple: The snow showed the bright blue color of the early-morning sky, so the snow also looked blue.
sentences.main: The snow itself looked blue.

parts.text: Reflecting the brilliant blue of the early-morning sky,
parts.meaning: Showing the bright blue of the sky early in the morning,
even the snow looked blue.

sentences.grammar: The -ing phrase at the start explains why. "Itself" adds force: "even the snow".

sentences.context: Gunnar Kaasen also glanced in their direction, but his eyes passed over them without interest.
sentences.simple: Gunnar Kaasen also looked quickly toward them, but he did not notice them.
sentences.main: Gunnar Kaasen glanced in their direction.

parts.text: Gunnar Kaasen also glanced in their direction,
parts.meaning: Gunnar Kaasen also looked quickly toward them,

parts.text: but his eyes passed over them without interest.
parts.meaning: but he looked past them and did not care.

sentences.grammar: "Glance in someone's direction" = look quickly toward them. "Without interest" = not interested.

sentences.context: Somehow the package had come untied from my sled.
sentences.simple: In some way I don't know, the package was no longer tied to my sled.
sentences.main: The package had come untied.

parts.meaning: In some way that I do not know,
the package had become untied
from my sled.

sentences.grammar: "Come untied" = become untied. "Somehow" = in a way you do not know.

sentences.context: What a disaster it would have been if the medicine were lost on the trail!
sentences.simple: It would have been terrible if the medicine had been lost on the trail!
sentences.main: What a disaster it would have been!

parts.text: What a disaster it would have been
parts.meaning: How terrible it would have been

parts.text: if the medicine were lost on the trail!
parts.meaning: if the medicine was lost on the trail!

sentences.grammar: "What a + noun + subject + verb!" is an exclamation. "Would have been" talks about a past thing that did not happen.

sentences.context: The hard work of all the mushers and dogs would have been for nothing.
sentences.simple: All the hard work of the mushers and dogs would have been wasted.
sentences.main: The hard work would have been for nothing.

parts.text: The hard work of all the mushers and dogs
parts.meaning: All the hard work of the mushers and dogs
would have had no result.

sentences.grammar: "Would have been" is the third conditional result: it did not happen. "For nothing" = with no result.

sentences.context: When they looked out the window, they were nearly blinded by the dazzling reflection of sunlight on the snow and the ice-covered sea.
sentences.simple: When they looked out the window, the very bright sunlight on the snow and ice almost stopped them from seeing.
sentences.main: They were nearly blinded.

parts.text: When they looked out the window,
parts.meaning: When they looked out of the window,
they almost could not see

parts.text: by the dazzling reflection of sunlight
parts.meaning: because of the very bright sunlight that came back

parts.text: on the snow and the ice-covered sea.
parts.meaning: from the snow and the frozen sea.

sentences.grammar: "Were blinded by" is passive; "by" shows the cause. "Nearly" = almost.

sentences.context: No time at all had passed in Frog Creek.
sentences.simple: In Frog Creek, no time had passed while they were away.
sentences.main: No time at all had passed.

parts.meaning: Not even a little time
had gone by in Frog Creek.

sentences.grammar: "At all" makes a negative stronger. "Had passed" is past perfect.

sentences.context: Jack reached out, and the next thing he knew, his hand was wet from puppy licks.
sentences.simple: Jack put his hand out, and very soon the puppy had licked it and made it wet.
sentences.main: His hand was wet from puppy licks.

parts.meaning: Jack put out his hand,

parts.text: and the next thing he knew,
parts.meaning: and suddenly,

parts.text: his hand was wet from puppy licks.
parts.meaning: his hand was wet because the puppy licked it.

sentences.grammar: "The next thing I knew" = very suddenly. "Wet from" shows the cause.

sentences.context: The nationwide attention given to their story helped raise awareness about the importance of widespread vaccines to prevent the disease.
sentences.simple: Because the whole country heard their story, more people understood how important it is for many people to get vaccines against the disease.
sentences.main: The attention helped raise awareness.

parts.meaning: The interest from the whole country
that their story got
helped more people know

parts.text: about the importance of widespread vaccines
parts.meaning: how important it is for many people to get vaccines
to stop the disease.

sentences.grammar: "Given to their story" is a past participle phrase = "that was given to their story". "Help + verb" (no "to").

sentences.context: So Kaasen decided to speed on to Nome to get the medicine there as soon as possible.
sentences.simple: So Kaasen chose to go fast on to Nome to bring the medicine there as quickly as he could.
sentences.main: Kaasen decided to speed on to Nome.

parts.meaning: So Kaasen chose
to go on quickly to Nome
to bring the medicine there
as quickly as he could.

sentences.grammar: "Decide to + verb". The second "to get..." tells the purpose.
